title: Capital: Value, Surplus Value and Crisis

cards.b: Capital (Volume 1, 1867) is the book most people cite and few read. Its question is simple: if markets exchange equal values, where does profit come from? Marx's answer, surplus value, is the theoretical core of the claim that capitalism rests on exploitation.

cards.h: From Smith and Ricardo to Marx
cards.b: Marx built on the classical economists. Adam Smith (Wealth of Nations, 1776) and David Ricardo (1817) held that the value of a good comes from labour. Marx wrote Volume 1 in London after years in the British Museum library. Engels edited Volumes 2 (1885) and 3 (1894) from Marx's notes after his death in 1883.

A commodity has use-value (usefulness) and exchange-value (what it trades for). Marx argues the value of commodities reflects the socially necessary labour time to produce them under average conditions. Money is the general form of value. Prices fluctuate, but over time they are ruled by labour content, he claims.

The worker sells labour power, not labour. Its price, the wage, equals the cost of keeping the worker alive. But in a working day the worker produces more value than that. If a worker covers wages in 4 hours of a 10-hour day, the other 6 hours yield surplus value, taken by the capitalist. The rate of exploitation is surplus value divided by variable capital (wages).

Exchange at the wage is fair on the surface; exploitation hides in the production process.

cards.h: Accumulation and the falling rate of profit
cards.b: Competition forces capitalists to invest in machines (constant capital). Since only living labour creates surplus value, Marx argues that a rising ratio of machines to labour tends to lower the rate of profit (Volume 3). Counter-forces exist: cheaper goods, longer hours, new markets. The industrial reserve army of unemployed keeps wages down. Capital concentrates into fewer, larger firms.

cards.h: Crisis and the end of capitalism
cards.b: Marx sees crises of overproduction and credit as built into the system: production expands faster than demand. Booms and slumps recur (1825, 1857, 1873...). In Volume 1 chapter 32 he predicts that "the expropriators are expropriated". He did not give a date, and in the Grundrisse (1857-58, published 1939-41) he even hints at automation reducing labour.

Real wages did rise in rich countries; Marx's "increasing misery" did not appear as a steady fall in living standards. But inequality fell in the mid-20th century, then rose again; Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) revived Marxian themes with data. Crises did recur: 1929, 2008. Concentration into giant firms is real. Yet capitalism proved adaptable through welfare states and credit.

Böhm-Bawerk (1896) pointed to the "transformation problem": Marx's values and actual prices of production do not match neatly. Marginalists (Jevons, Menger, 1870s) say value comes from subjective utility, not labour. Okishio's theorem (1961) shows that cost-cutting innovation need not lower the profit rate. Joan Robinson thought the labour theory unnecessary; Analytical Marxists (Roemer) say exploitation can be defined without it. Hayek says prices carry information that labour times cannot.

Dadabhai Naoroji's drain theory (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901) and R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India (1901-03) anticipate imperialism critiques. Post-Independence, P.C. Mahalanobis's Second Five-Year Plan (1956) drew on Soviet planning. Marxist economists such as Prabhat Patnaik and Utsa Patnaik (Capital and Imperialism, 2021) continue the Marxian tradition; "Capital" was also the prop of arguments over agrarian classes (Mode of Production debate, 1970s).

Key takeaways

  1. Value is socially necessary labour time; labour power is the commodity workers sell.
  2. Surplus value arises from unpaid surplus labour.
  3. Accumulation raises machinery and may lower the rate of profit.
  4. Crises are recurrent; Marx foresaw concentration and the "expropriation of the expropriators".
  5. The transformation problem and marginalism challenge the labour theory.

Debate questions

  1. Does exploitation require the labour theory of value?
  2. Have welfare states disproved Marx's predictions or only postponed them?
